title: CVEs published
definition: CVE records grouped by NVD 'published' date, excluding records with status Rejected.
notes: 2026 is year-to-date; it already exceeds all of 2025 by about 72% with roughly 2.5 months left, and the cause has not been established from the source. Counts by NVD published date, excluding Rejected records. Cross-checked: CVE.ICU (built from the same NVD feed) matches 2006–2025 exactly; Jerry Gamblin's year-end reviews are within 0.1% for 2023–2025. The 2017 step change coincides with CVE Numbering Authorities growing from 24 (start of 2016) to 78 (2017), per a 2023 NIST/CVE program presentation; fits start at 2017 by default.
why: Watch whether the 2026 jump persists into a full year and appears in KEV too. A sustained break would be one of several possible explanations to test, including NVD processing changes, CNA growth, and AI-assisted discovery.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: CVE.ICU yearly summary (exact match 2006–2025); Gamblin 2023/2024/2025 reviews (≤0.1%); 2026 YTD within 0.4% of CVE.ICU live count.

title: CISA KEV additions
unit_label: Known Exploited Vulnerabilities added per year
definition: KEV catalog entries grouped by year of dateAdded. Auto-refreshed weekly on GitHub.
notes: 2021 covers Nov 3–Dec 31 only (launch backlog) and 2022 includes a large backfill of older exploited CVEs, so fits start at 2023 by default. Few full years, so forecasts stay short.
why: KEV lists CVEs that CISA has reliable evidence are being exploited and that have clear remediation guidance. It is a subset of all exploited CVEs, so absence from KEV does not mean a CVE is unexploited.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: recounted from cisagov/kev-data (catalog 2026.10.16, 1,748 entries).

title: KEV additions vs CVEs
unit_label: KEV entries added ÷ CVEs published, same calendar year
source_name: Derived from CISA KEV and NIST NVD (rows above)
definition: KEV entries added in a year divided by CVEs published in that year, as a percentage. Computed, not reported by any source.
notes: A ratio of yearly flows: KEV additions include CVEs published in earlier years, so this is not the share of a year's CVEs later exploited. Starts at 2023 because 2021 was a partial launch year and 2022 is inflated by the initial KEV backfill. Year-to-date values are excluded. Only three full years, so treat any forecast as indicative.
why: A falling ratio means CVE disclosure volume is growing faster than KEV additions. KEV additions depend on CISA's evidence and listing criteria, not only on exploitation.
verification: Computed from the two verified series above.

title: ICS advisories
unit_label: CISA ICS + medical advisory rows per year (ICS Advisory Project)
definition: CISA/ICS-CERT industrial control system advisories (ICSA + ICSMA medical), counted as rows of the ICS Advisory Project master dataset grouped by its 'Year' column.
notes: Rows are not unique advisories: 4,074 rows vs 4,031 unique advisory numbers (3,877 ICSA rows, 197 ICSMA). The 'Year' column differs from the release year for 124 rows; counting by release date gives e.g. 2021 = 405, 2025 = 502. 2010 is a partial program year and excluded from fits. Auto-refreshed weekly from the dataset.
why: A public proxy for the rate at which vulnerabilities in industrial control products are being disclosed.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: independent recount of the raw CSV matched all 17 years.

title: Ransomware leak-site victims
unit_label: victims posted on leak sites per year
definition: Victims posted on ransomware data-leak sites tracked by ransomware.live, by year of posting.
notes: 2020 reflects limited tracker coverage and is excluded from fits. Counts differ by tracker and are revised as sites are re-scraped. Yearly pages at ransomware.live/stats/YYYY, retrieved 2026-10-20.
why: An incomplete and noisy indicator: victims who pay or are never posted are missing, and posts can include duplicates or false claims. Useful for direction and scale, not as a census.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: each year confirmed on ransomware.live/stats/YYYY.

title: US data compromises
unit_label: publicly reported US data compromises per year
source_name: Identity Theft Resource Center, 2025 Annual Data Breach Report (Appendix A)
definition: Publicly reported US data compromises (breaches, exposures, leaks, unspecified) tracked by ITRC per calendar year.
notes: All years from the 2025 report's year-over-year table, which revises earlier releases (e.g., 2023 was first reported as 3,205 and 2022 as 1,801). Table read from a re-hosted copy of the PDF; ITRC's own page confirms 2023–2025.
why: Counts compromise events, not individuals affected. ITRC's Q3 2023 report counted MOVEit-related compromises among the year's largest (79 organizations directly and 344 through vendors as of September 30, 2023).
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: all 20 values against the 2025 report table; 2023–2025 also on ITRC's site. MOVEit figures from ITRC's Q3 2023 report (idtheftcenter.org).

title: FBI IC3 reported losses
unit_label: victim losses reported to IC3 per year
source_name: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center annual reports
definition: Total victim losses reported in complaints to IC3 during the calendar year.
notes: 2010: IC3 published no loss estimate for 2010, so it is blank. 2008 ($265M) is the FBI's rounded figure. 2012 uses the figure restated in the 2013 report ($581.4M; the 2012 report said $525.4M). 2012–2014 are 'adjusted' losses. 2020 and 2022 use the report charts ($4.2B, $10.3B); the report text says 'exceeding $4.1 billion' and 'more than $10.2 billion'. The FBI's 2016 report estimated that only about 15% of fraud victims report their crimes.
why: Shown on a log scale; the board picks the best-fitting model automatically. A break from trend could reflect a real shift or a change in how losses are reported.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: against each year's IC3 report PDF (2006–2009 via IC3 public service announcements).

title: FBI IC3 complaints
source_name: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center annual reports
definition: Number of complaints received by IC3 in the calendar year.
notes: From 2020 to 2025 complaints rose about 27% (791,790 to 1,008,597) while reported losses rose about 5x ($4.2B to $20.9B).
why: When losses grow much faster than complaints, the average reported loss is rising. That may reflect a shift toward higher-loss fraud types, larger reported losses, or reporting changes.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: against IC3 reports' year-by-year charts and each year's report.

title: IC3 loss per complaint
source_name: Derived from FBI IC3 annual reports (rows above)
definition: Total reported losses divided by total complaints for the same year. Computed, not reported by IC3; many complaints report no loss, so this is an average across all complaints.
notes: Inherits all IC3 caveats, including the 2012–2014 'adjusted' losses. 2010 is blank because IC3 published no 2010 loss figure.
why: Rising loss per complaint means the average reported loss per complaint is growing. It does not by itself say why.
verification: Computed from the two verified IC3 series above.

title: GPS signal loss in airline ops
unit_label: GPS loss events per 1,000 flights (IATA FDX)
source_name: IATA FDX via GNSS-RFI Safety Risk Assessment v6 (Feb 2026)
definition: GPS signal loss events per 1,000 flights recorded by FDX member operators from aircraft ADS-B data.
notes: All five values are data labels on Figure 2 of IATA's GNSS interference safety risk assessment (v6, Feb 2026), matched to years by the chart's axis order. IATA's December 2025 statements (via press) give 31 for 2022 and 56 for 2024, consistent with the chart. 2025 (57.1) is marked provisional by IATA; IATA's December 2025 estimate for 2025 was 59. 2021 covers Aug–Dec only and is excluded from fits. Measures GPS signal loss from any cause; IATA gives no breakdown by cause and publishes no comparable annual spoofing count.
why: A consistent public measure of GPS signal loss in airline operations, which is where electronic interference meets flight safety.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: chart labels confirmed in the IATA PDF; year pairing by axis order.

title: Industrial robots installed
unit_label: new industrial robots installed worldwide per year
source_name: International Federation of Robotics, World Robotics
definition: Industrial robots installed (shipped) worldwide in the calendar year, per IFR.
notes: IFR revises earlier years; each value is the newest IFR figure found (2013–2017 from World Robotics 2019 Table 2.1; 2016 and 2017 revised up from the first-published 294,000 and 381,000). 2006–2012 are rounded to thousands. 2009 is the financial-crisis dip and is excluded from fits. Operational stock passed 5 million in 2025 (5,079,078). IFR forecasts 655,000 installations for 2026.
why: A rough proxy for growth in networked automation equipment on factory floors, part of the OT attack surface.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: against IFR World Robotics executive summaries 2020–2026 and WR2019 Table 2.1; 2016 and 2017 corrected.

title: Frontier AI training compute
unit_label: largest training compute of a notable model released that year
source_name: Epoch AI (2010–2022 via Our World in Data; 2023–2026 Epoch frontier models)
definition: Highest estimated training compute (FLOP) of any notable/frontier model published in the calendar year.
notes: Most values are Epoch estimates, not disclosed figures. 2026 covers releases through Sep 30; GPT-6 Astra's value is estimated from reported hardware (90% range about 5e26–2e27), and two later GPT-6 models have no estimate yet, so the 2026 maximum may change. Per-year maxima are noisy (2017 and 2024 dip below the prior year). Epoch measured frontier training-compute growth at 4–5x per year for 2010 to May 2024; it has not published that rate for later years. 2017's maximum (JFT, 8.43e20) reflects Epoch's current estimate of AlphaGo Zero (6.49e20). OpenAI's 2018 'AI and Compute' analysis described a 300,000-fold compute increase from AlexNet to AlphaGo Zero, implying a much larger AlphaGo Zero figure; the sources' estimation methods differ, and the board uses Epoch's throughout.
why: Training compute is one of the main inputs Epoch tracks for AI capability. Growth here signals what defenders may soon need to verify and oversee.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: 2010–2025 match Our World in Data's Epoch-based chart; 2026 from Epoch's frontier models file.

title: Cyber workforce gap
unit_label: ISC2 estimate of unfilled positions worldwide
definition: ISC2's estimate of additional cybersecurity professionals needed worldwide to adequately staff organizations.
notes: Rounded headline figures (exact: 2022 = 3,432,476; 2024 = 4,763,963). 2018 is confirmed only through trade-press coverage of ISC2's release. The 2025 study contains no global gap figure (ISC2's 2025 pages show none; trade press reported the omission). The series has effectively ended and stays here as context. ISC2's methodology changed across editions, so year-to-year moves are not strictly comparable.
why: ISC2's 2025 study shifted emphasis from headcount shortages to skills gaps (as reported by trade press, December 2025). Watch which measure replaces this one.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: against ISC2 releases (2019–2024) and trade press (2018, 2025).

title: Cyber workforce size
unit_label: ISC2 estimate of people working in cybersecurity worldwide
definition: ISC2's estimate of the number of people working in cybersecurity worldwide.
notes: Rounded figures (exact: 2022 = 4,656,084; 2024 = 5,468,173). 2019 is confirmed only through trade-press coverage. Essentially flat from 2023 to 2024. No 2025 figure published.
why: Workforce growth stalling while threat volume climbs is the setup for automation, and for people who can supervise it.
verification: Independently re-verified 2026-10-20: against ISC2 releases (2020–2024) and trade press (2019).
